disease_info: Delusional disorder is characterized by one or more persistent, non-bizarre or somewhat plausible delusions lasting at least one month, in the absence of prominent hallucinations, disorganized thought, or marked functional decline typical of schizophrenia. Outside the delusional themes, individuals often appear relatively intact, with preserved cognition, affect, and daily functioning, which can delay detection and treatment. Onset is typically in mid-to-late adulthood and may follow psychosocial stressors, interpersonal conflicts, or situations that can be misinterpreted and woven into a fixed false belief. It is distinguished from mood and psychotic disorders by the circumscribed nature of the beliefs, minimal other psychotic features, and relatively stable overall functioning.

narrative.personality: Andrew is a meticulous, visually oriented and introspective professional who balances structured analytical work with solitary creative pursuits like painting, poetry, and gardening.
narrative.stressor: About eighteen months ago, Andrew’s firm underwent a leadership change and began aggressively pushing new cost-cutting targets and tighter bidding timelines, placing intense scrutiny on his estimates and introducing a new project management system he privately doubted. A contentious hospital project, where several unexpected site conditions led to overruns, resulted in repeated questioning of his models by management and a formal review of his past bids, which he experienced as a personal attack on his integrity and professional identity. He started poring obsessively over emails, meeting notes, and project data at home, trying to reconcile perceived inconsistencies, and gradually interpreted ordinary managerial oversight and software glitches as evidence of a coordinated effort to undermine or scapegoat him. Over the following year, this fixed interpretation solidified despite colleagues’ reassurances and an overall satisfactory performance review, and after his wife and a trusted coworker noticed how preoccupied and inflexible he had become about these beliefs and how much it was straining his sleep and home life, they persuaded him to see a psychiatrist.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’m here because I have these beliefs about what’s going on at work that nobody can talk me out of, no matter what they show me.”

narrative.personality: Jose is a calm, disciplined, and highly skilled welder who takes pride in his craftsmanship, competitiveness, and devotion to family and practical routines.
narrative.stressor: Roughly two years ago, Jose experienced a minor workplace accident where he briefly lost consciousness after being struck by a falling piece of metal, followed by several weeks of headaches and dizziness that were evaluated in the emergency department and deemed without serious findings. Although he initially returned to work, he remained uneasy about his health, reading articles and watching documentaries about long-term effects of head injuries and industrial exposures, and he began to fixate on the idea that something had been missed or was being hidden from him. Routine follow-up visits and normal test results did not reassure him; instead, he increasingly interpreted medical explanations and paperwork errors as signs that doctors, his employer, and even the workers’ compensation insurer were concealing a serious condition or using him as part of some undisclosed study. Over the course of a year, this belief hardened despite his wife’s attempts to accompany him to appointments and clarify what was said, and only after he started refusing recommended procedures, arguing with supervisors about supposed hidden health risks, and his family doctor noted how immovable his ideas had become did they convince him to accept a referral to psychiatric care.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep holding on to these ideas about my health and what the doctors and company are doing, and nobody can convince me they’re wrong.”

narrative.personality: Valerie is a methodical, intellectually curious, and somewhat solitary person who channels her energy into precision work, self-improvement, and quiet hobbies like reading, gardening, and meditation.
narrative.stressor: About a year and a half ago, Valerie’s younger sister moved back to their hometown and into a closer relationship with their aging parents, leading to renewed family tensions that Valerie had largely avoided by living independently and focusing on her career. Long-standing feelings of being overlooked in the family resurfaced as her parents began asking her sister, rather than her, for help with decisions, while at work she was passed over for a supervisory training opportunity she had been informally preparing for. She started ruminating extensively about these slights and spending evenings replaying conversations, gradually coming to see routine family disagreements and ambiguous comments from coworkers as confirming a specific, fixed interpretation of how others were treating her that she could not let go of despite their explanations and alternative perspectives. Over the following year, this rigid view began to color her interactions, straining family gatherings and workplace relationships, and after a trusted coworker from her yoga group gently pointed out how stuck she seemed on these beliefs and suggested that it might help to talk to a professional, Valerie agreed to seek psychiatric consultation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel like I’ve gotten locked into certain beliefs about how people are treating me, and I can’t shake them even when they try to explain otherwise.”
